rows.why: The tasks each agent performs and the chains of actions, tools and systems it uses to do them are defined and documented.
The agent's knowledge limits, the conditions outside its intended use, and how its output is used and overseen by humans are documented.
The scope of what each agent may do on its own is specified: which systems, which actions, which data, and which actions are never left to it.
Human oversight of agent actions is defined: which steps need approval or review, who does it, and how it is trained and assessed.

The components an agent is built on (models, orchestration frameworks, libraries, executors) are identified and held to approved, controlled versions, with their legal and supply-chain risks documented.
The likelihood and magnitude of harm from agent actions are assessed, including irreversible changes and actions triggered by manipulated input.
Privacy risk from the data an agent reads, keeps in memory and passes between tools is examined, including redaction in logs.
Agent behaviour in production is monitored for unexpected action chains, tool use and drift from what was approved.
The agent is shown to complete its tasks correctly and reliably under realistic conditions, and the limits of where it can be trusted are documented.
Agents are tested under stress and unexpected conditions to show they fail safely, with loops and runaway action chains stopped.
Agent security is tested with adversarial and red-team exercises, including manipulated input that triggers actions and attempts to break out of the sandbox.
Agent actions, tool calls and the identity used are logged and kept so what an agent did can be traced and reviewed.
An agent's decisions and action chains can be explained, documented and interpreted in context, so reviewers understand why it acted.
Staff and others can report agent misbehaviour and unexpected actions, and these reports feed how the agent is evaluated.
Feedback from operators and users, and how often staff override the agent, are used to judge whether it performs as intended.
Results are used to decide whether the agent achieves its purpose and whether its autonomy should continue, be reduced or be stopped.
Controls limit what an agent can do: least-privilege identities, sandboxing, approval for high-impact or irreversible steps, and limits on rate and cost.
Agent-specific incidents are responded to and recovered from, including reversing the changes an agent made.
An agent can be stopped, bypassed or its access revoked quickly when it acts outside its intended use, and who may do so is assigned.
Post-deployment monitoring of agents covers staff override, change management of agent configuration and tools, and retirement of agents.
Agent incidents and errors are recorded, communicated to those affected and reviewed for root cause.

review.reason: Folded MAP 4.1 is not fully asked: the why says 'legal and supply-chain risks documented' but not third-party IP/rights infringement or the inventory of third-party material; AGENT-16.4 (third-party component inventory) supports it and is missing.
AGENT-16.6 is a vulnerability severity rating process, not evidence for likelihood and magnitude of harm from agent actions; drop it.

Redaction in logs and the log CIS refs (AGENT-8.1, 8.5) belong to Input (prompt and response logs); privacy of data passed between tools overlaps Input, Source data and MCP/tools; the row reads as generic privacy.

Showing the agent answers correctly and reliably is accuracy/consistency TEVV, done at Output for everyone; keep only if reworded to agent task completion and limits of autonomy; empty cis_refs although AGENT-16.13 (evaluation harnesses, adversarial inputs) supports it.
Largely repeats MEASURE 2.8 (what the agent did, traced from logs); AGENT-8.5/8.11 are the same evidence; no distinct explainability check for this area.
Staff override is the same check as MEASURE 4.2 (override frequency); the why also mixes change management and retirement, so it asks several things; AGENT-8.11 log review does not support override.
Nothing checks agent performance and assurance criteria measured under conditions like the real deployment (real systems, messy inputs, non-optimised conditions); AGENT-16.13 supports it.
Nothing asks what benefit justifies giving the agent autonomy (time saved, error rates against a human baseline) as examined with its users.
The row limits rate and cost, which harms spend/assets; the area's impacts (access, process, data) may be too narrow.
